title: Time-of-day-dependent effects of bright light exposure on human psychophysiology: comparison of daytime and nighttime exposure
research_question: To determine whether the immediate psychophysiological effects of bright light exposure (on sleepiness, fatigue, energy, core body temperature, cortisol, and heart rate) are dependent on the time of day (daytime vs. nighttime exposure).

participants.description: 24 healthy, nonsmoking young males (18-30 yr), with intermediate Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire scores. 12 subjects in daytime experiment (mean age 23.1 ± 1.5 yr), 12 subjects in nighttime experiment (mean age 21.8 ± 1.9 yr).
participants.recruitment: Subjects were screened using a general health questionnaire and a Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Bright light exposure (5,000 lux) or dim light exposure (<10 lux, control condition) for 4 hours. Light was provided by Bright Light boxes placed vertically in front of a computer screen. Subjects remained seated and were instructed to look at the light source regularly. During dim light, lamps were off.

measures.instrument: Electrocardiogram (ECG) using disposable, single-use, pregelled electrodes (Red Dot; 3M Health Care, Borken, Germany), bipolar Wilson lead (V6 and right collarbone)
Saliva samples analyzed by RIA (Spectria, 125I-labeled cortisol, Coated Tube Radioimmunoassay; Orion Diagnostics, Espoo, Finland)
Rectal probe connected to a portable registration system (JOBLOG)

findings.antecedent: Bright light exposure (5,000 lux) during nighttime (midnight-4:00 A.M.)
findings.mechanism: Light exposure at night influences autonomic nervous system activity.
findings.quote: Post hoc ANOVAS showed that bright light exposure significantly increased heart rate during nighttime [F(1,11) = 22.9, P = 0.001]

findings.antecedent: Bright light exposure (5,000 lux) during daytime (noon-4:00 P.M.)
findings.mechanism: The effect of bright light on heart rate is time-of-day dependent.
Cortisol production is usually low during nighttime, and daytime exposure timing (noon-4PM) might be too late to affect the morning cortisol peak.
findings.quote: Light had no significant effect on cortisol [interaction effect for the factors condition and exposure, F(1,22) = 0.9, P > 0.1], independent of the time of day

findings.antecedent: Bright light exposure (5,000 lux) during nighttime (midnight-4:00 A.M.)
findings.mechanism: Bright light exposure at night enhances core body temperature, consistent with previous findings.
findings.quote: Post hoc ANOVAs revealed that CBT increased in bright light exposure compared with dim light during nighttime [F(1,6) = 6.1, P = 0.048]

findings.antecedent: Bright light exposure (5,000 lux) during daytime (noon-4:00 P.M.)
findings.mechanism: The effect of bright light on CBT is time-of-day dependent.
Bright light has an alerting effect, reducing subjective sleepiness.
findings.quote: a clear reduction of subjective sleepiness as measured by the KSS for the daytime and nighttime bright light exposure [interaction effect for the factors condition and exposure, F(1,22) = 16.8, P < 0.001].

findings.mechanism: The alerting effect of bright light is independent of the time of day.
findings.quote: This alerting effect of bright light exposure is independent of the time of day at which light is presented [3-way interaction effect for the factors condition, exposure, and experiment, F(1,22) = 0.4, P = 0.527].

subjects in the bright light group report that they feel less fatigued during the light exposure than before compared with the dim light group [interaction effect for factors condition and exposure, F(1,22) = 8.3, P = 0.008].

findings.mechanism: The effect of bright light on subjective fatigue is independent of the time of day.
findings.quote: As for subjective sleepiness, the effect of bright light on subjective fatigue is independent of time of day [3-way interaction of condition, exposure, and experiment, F(1,22) = 0.8, P = 0.372].

findings.mechanism: Bright light tends to increase subjective energy.
findings.quote: This interaction effect of condition and exposure was not significant [F(1,22) = 3.6, P = 0.071].

findings.mechanism: The effect of bright light on subjective energy is independent of the time of day.
findings.quote: Again the effect was independent of the time the light was given [F(1,22) = 0.4, P = 0.503].

mechanisms: The paper suggests an alternative mechanism for light's alerting effects beyond melatonin suppression, possibly involving indirect projections from the SCN to brain areas associated with sleep-wake regulation (e.g., locus coeruleus, ventrolateral preoptic nucleus).
The similarity of sleepiness-reducing effects of light in the night and during the day partially results from increased sleep pressure due to restricted sleep duration in experiment A.
moderators: Time of day (daytime vs. nighttime exposure)
implementation_implications: The psychological benefits of bright light (reduced sleepiness, fatigue, increased energy) are consistent regardless of whether it's applied during the day or night, suggesting broad applicability for improving alertness and performance.
Physiological responses (heart rate, CBT) to bright light are time-of-day dependent, implying that applications targeting these physiological changes should consider timing.

tables.description: Experimental design of the two experiments (daytime and nighttime bright light exposure), showing wake periods, sleeping periods, and periods of light exposure/dim light control, along with continuous and hourly measurement timings.

Course of heart rate, cortisol concentration, and core body temperature for daytime and nighttime experiments, before and during bright light exposure vs. dim light. Includes statistical significances for condition effects and time-of-day dependency.
key_stats: Heart rate: F(1,22)=13.0, p=0.002 (condition x exposure), F(1,22)=7.9, p=0.010 (condition x exposure x experiment)
CBT: F(1,15)=4.5, p=0.05 (condition x exposure), F(1,15)=7.2, p=0.017 (condition x exposure x experiment)

tables.description: Course of subjective sleepiness, fatigue, and energy for daytime and nighttime experiments, before and during bright light exposure vs. dim light. Includes statistical significances for condition effects and time-of-day dependency.
key_stats: Sleepiness: F(1,22)=16.8, p<0.001 (condition x exposure), F(1,22)=0.4, p=0.527 (condition x exposure x experiment)
Fatigue: F(1,22)=8.3, p=0.008 (condition x exposure), F(1,22)=0.8, p=0.372 (condition x exposure x experiment)
Energy: F(1,22)=3.6, p=0.071 (condition x exposure), F(1,22)=0.4, p=0.503 (condition x exposure x experiment)

limitations: The comparison includes only two circadian phases (daytime and nighttime) and a limited number of variables.

The similarity of sleepiness suppressive effects of light in the night and during the day might partially result from increased sleep pressure due to restricted sleep duration (7 h) on the adaptation night in experiment A.

paper_metadata.title: Time-of-day-dependent effects of bright light exposure on human psychophysiology: comparison of daytime and nighttime exposure.
paper_metadata.journal: American Journal of Physiology. Regulatory Integrative and Comparative Physiology
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Time-of-day-dependent effects of bright light exposure on human psychophysiology: comparison of daytime and nighttime exposure
paper_metadata.crossref_journal: American Journal of Physiology-Regulatory, Integrative and Comparative Physiology
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Bright light can influence human psychophysiology instantaneously by inducing endocrine (suppression of melatonin, increasing cortisol levels), other physiological changes (enhancement of core body temperature), and psychological changes (reduction of sleepiness, increase of alertness). Its broad range of action is reflected in the wide field of applications, ranging from optimizing a work environment to treating depressed patients. For optimally applying bright light and understanding its mechanism, it is crucial to know whether its effects depend on the time of day. In this paper, we report the effects of bright light given at two different times of day on psychological and physiological parameters. Twenty-four subjects participated in two experiments ( n = 12 each). All subjects were nonsmoking, healthy young males (18–30 yr). In both experiments, subjects were exposed to either bright light (5,000 lux) or dim light <10 lux (control condition) either between 12:00 P.M. and 4:00 P.M. ( experiment A) or between midnight and 4:00 A.M. ( experiment B). Hourly measurements included salivary cortisol concentrations, electrocardiogram, sleepiness (Karolinska Sleepiness Scale), fatigue, and energy ratings (Visual Analog Scale). Core body temperature was measured continuously throughout the experiments. Bright light had a time-dependent effect on heart rate and core body temperature; i.e., bright light exposure at night, but not in daytime, increased heart rate and enhanced core body temperature. It had no significant effect at all on cortisol. The effect of bright light on the psychological variables was time independent, since nighttime and daytime bright light reduced sleepiness and fatigue significantly and similarly.
